title: Do outcomes track who lives in the neighborhood?
question: Across neighborhoods, do refusals, withdrawals, neighbors’ objections and lost homes rise or fall with income, renting, race and ethnicity, birthplace or age of the residents?
finding: Counted plainly, no resident characteristic is linked to the share of applications not approved beyond what chance would produce (income -0.37 across 28 neighborhoods). Once every neighborhood is given the same mix of proposals, non-approval is lower where incomes are higher: rank correlation -0.52 (moderate), -0.58 measured against each neighborhood’s own mix, and -0.57 when the share filed through firms is also made equal - all three beyond chance. Measured against its own mix only, the link also shows for the share of white residents (-0.55), the share born abroad (+0.58); those do not hold in the like-for-like rate. Using a firm to file does not explain it: the share of applications filed through a named firm has no link with income (-0.05). Neighbors’ requests for a review are the strongest pattern: the share of white residents +0.63; household income +0.61; the share below the poverty line -0.61; the share of Asian residents -0.53 (26 neighborhoods).
how: Each neighborhood’s rates from the table above are set beside its Census profile (2020-24 survey, tracts added up to neighborhoods; income is the household-weighted average of tract medians). The figure is a rank correlation: +1 means the two rise together in perfect order, 0 means no relation, -1 means one falls as the other rises. Under 0.2 is called no link, 0.2-0.4 weak, 0.4-0.6 moderate, above 0.6 strong. Three versions of the non-approval rate are shown: as counted; with every neighborhood given the same mix of proposals; and the count set against what the neighborhood’s own cases would produce at citywide rates. “Chance” is judged at about the 1-in-100 level. Areas only: nothing is known or assumed about any applicant.
limits: A difference between places is not proof of bias. Places differ in what is proposed, in zoning, lot sizes, building ages and land prices, and in who chooses to apply at all; applicants also withdraw for their own reasons (money, a sale, a redesign filed under a new number). A link across areas says nothing about how any single applicant was treated, and resident characteristics move together (income, renting, race and age are tangled), so no one of them can be singled out as the cause. About 70 comparisons are made here, so a few will look notable by luck; only a link that holds in every version of the rate deserves weight. Wealthier owners can also afford to file, object and appeal more often. The hearing minutes, roll-call votes and appeal decisions now being collected would show who voted, who objected and what reason was recorded in each case.
